{{Short description|Mathematical Model}}
[[File:Lamb-Chaplygin_dipole.png|alt=|thumb|300x300px|The flow structure of the Lamb-Chaplygin dipole]]
The '''Lamb–Chaplygin dipole''' model is a mathematical description for a particular inviscid and steady dipolar vortex flow. It is a non-trivial solution to the two-dimensional [[Euler equations (fluid dynamics)|Euler equations]]. The model is named after [[Horace Lamb]] and [[Sergey Alexeyevich Chaplygin]], who independently discovered this flow structure.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Meleshko|first1=V. V.|last2=Heijst|first2=G. J. F. van|date=August 1994|title=On Chaplygin's investigations of two-dimensional vortex structures in an inviscid fluid|journal=Journal of Fluid Mechanics|language=en|volume=272|pages=157–182|doi=10.1017/S0022112094004428|bibcode=1994JFM...272..157M |s2cid=123008925 |issn=1469-7645}}</ref> This dipole is the two-dimensional analogue of [[Hill's spherical vortex]].
__TOC__

==The model==
A two-dimensional (2D), [[solenoidal vector field]] <math> \mathbf{u} </math> may be described by a scalar [[stream function]] <math>\psi</math>, via <math>\mathbf{u} = -\mathbf{e_z} \times \mathbf{\nabla} \psi</math>, where <math>\mathbf{e_z}</math> is the right-handed unit vector perpendicular to the 2D plane. By definition, the stream function is related to the [[vorticity]] <math>\omega</math> via a [[Poisson equation]]:  <math>-\nabla^2\psi = \omega</math>. The Lamb–Chaplygin model follows from demanding the following characteristics: {{citation needed|date=March 2020}}

* The dipole has a circular atmosphere/separatrix with radius <math>R</math>: <math>\psi\left(r = R\right) = 0</math>.
* The dipole propages through an otherwise irrotational fluid (<math>\omega(r > R) = 0)</math> at translation velocity <math>U</math>.    
* The flow is steady in the co-moving frame of reference: <math>\omega (r < R) = f\left(\psi\right)</math>.
* Inside the atmosphere, there is a linear relation between the vorticity and the stream function <math>\omega = k^2 \psi </math>

The solution <math>\psi</math> in [[cylindrical coordinates]] (<math>r, \theta</math>), in the co-moving frame of reference reads:

<math>
\begin{align}
\psi =
\begin{cases}
\frac{-2 U J_{1}(kr)}{kJ_{0}(kR)}\mathrm{sin}(\theta) , & \text{for } r < R, \\ 
U\left(\frac{R^2}{r}-r\right)\mathrm{sin}(\theta), & \text{for } r \geq R, 
\end {cases}
\end{align}
</math>

where <math>J_0 \text{ and } J_1</math> are the zeroth and first [[Bessel functions]] of the first kind, respectively. Further, the value of <math>k</math> is such that <math> kR = 3.8317...</math>, the first non-trivial zero of the first Bessel function of the first kind.{{citation needed|date=March 2020}}

==Usage and considerations==
Since the seminal work of P. Orlandi,<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Orlandi|first=Paolo|date=August 1990|title=Vortex dipole rebound from a wall|journal=Physics of Fluids A: Fluid Dynamics|language=en|volume=2|issue=8|pages=1429–1436|doi=10.1063/1.857591|bibcode=1990PhFlA...2.1429O |issn=0899-8213}}</ref> the Lamb–Chaplygin vortex model has been a popular choice for numerical studies on vortex-environment interactions. The fact that it does not deform make it a prime candidate for consistent flow initialization. A less favorable property is that the second derivative of the flow field at the dipole's edge is not continuous.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Kizner|first1=Z.|last2=Khvoles|first2=R.|date=2004|title=Two variations on the theme of Lamb–Chaplygin: supersmooth dipole and rotating multipoles|journal=Regular and Chaotic Dynamics|volume=9|issue=4|pages=509|doi=10.1070/rd2004v009n04abeh000293|issn=1560-3547}}</ref> Further, it serves a framework for stability analysis on dipolar-vortex structures.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Brion|first1=V.|last2=Sipp|first2=D.|last3=Jacquin|first3=L.|date=2014-06-01|title=Linear dynamics of the Lamb-Chaplygin dipole in the two-dimensional limit|journal=Physics of Fluids|volume=26|issue=6|pages=064103|doi=10.1063/1.4881375|bibcode=2014PhFl...26f4103B |issn=1070-6631|url=https://hal.archives-ouvertes.fr/hal-01100934/file/DAFE14028.1418984393.pdf}}</ref>
